claims.text: The corrosion resistance of nuclear- and chemical-processing steels is primarily caused by a self-healing, chromium-enriched oxide passivation layer.
The chromium-enriched passivation layer forms and repairs itself under operational conditions.
The passive layer provides a protective barrier against corrosive agents.
The relevant nuclear- and chemical-processing grade steels contain sufficient chromium to support passivation.
Chromium chelators can inhibit reformation of the passive film.
A continuously forming, self-healing chromium oxide film adheres to the steel surface.
Residual chromium in the alloy migrates to the surface under corrosive conditions.
Surface chromium oxidizes to form a dense, adherent Cr2O3 layer.
The Cr2O3 layer impedes further corrosion.
Local damage to the passive layer is rapidly repaired through continued chromium oxidation.
Samples allowed to regenerate their passive film will have lower corrosion current densities than samples in which passive-film formation is inhibited.
Samples allowed to regenerate their passive film will exhibit less overall film degradation than samples in which passive-film formation is inhibited.
Samples allowed to regenerate their passive film will lose less weight than samples in which passive-film formation is inhibited.
The proposed mechanism applies under moderate pH, temperature, and radiation conditions typical of chemical-processing and nuclear-power operation.
The proposed mechanism may cease to apply under extreme mechanical wear or when passive-film formation is completely prevented.
Other alloying elements, including Mo, Ni, and Cu, may contribute to corrosion resistance.
Radiation-induced microstructural changes may influence corrosion resistance.
